Good morning class. We have five more classes in the semester, with the last four being the most important. Today, I will set up the background and context for these final sessions by reviewing what we've learned so far.

We discussed the Roman Republic, which was an oligarchy—rule by a few families. These families were called the Patricians. Despite Rome's small size, poverty, and ongoing wars at this time, everyone knew each other, creating an open, energetic, and cohesive society. Over time, the Roman Republic became dominant in the Mediterranean, defeating Carthage and the Greeks.

However, as Rome grew into an empire, the oligarchic structure became a problem. The fact that it was corrupt, unequal, and stagnant led to significant issues. For instance, Roman women began refusing to have children, leading to population decline. At this juncture, Rome should have established a centralized bureaucratic system for better empire management. However, because the powerful families refused to give up power, the empire remained divided among different family territories, resulting in constant civil wars.

Civil war started with Sulla and continued through Julius Caesar, whose successor Augustus became the first among equals but still failed to establish the necessary bureaucracy. This led to ongoing conflict. Eventually, Constantine realized this system was unsustainable and decided to reinvent Rome by moving the capital to a new location called Constantinople, which later became the Byzantine Empire. The language of the empire became Greek, creating a Greek-speaking bureaucratic state known as the second Rome.

Simultaneously, massive migrations of steppe people into Europe occurred due to conflicts in China between the Han dynasty and steppe nomadic peoples, forcing them westward and into Central Asia. These migrants posed a significant problem for Rome, which divided and ruled by absorbing many of them into the army as mercenaries to defend borders and fight civil wars.

In this context, we revisited the rise of the Catholic Church, supported by some noble families. This church system allowed war leaders from the migrants to become nobility, joining the 50 families to form a new elite class. At this point, Rome was set to divide into two parts: the western and eastern halves, each with distinct fates.
